note: Rewritten to the claim that survived the four independent audits.

problems.original_statement: Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person who is eligible at many points contributes to many trials. This uses the data better than a single baseline emulation and it introduces three complications together. The same person appears in many nested trials, so the observations are dependent in a way the pooled analysis must handle. Trials begun at different calendar times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so calendar time confounds the pooled contrast unless it is modeled. And a person's later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, which links the trials causally rather than merely statistically. The efficiency gain is real and it is what makes these complications easy to overlook.
problems.correction_note: The variance half of the claim is answered. Confidence-interval procedures for sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes have been compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, with the last recommended in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. The entry asked for that work as though it had not been done. What survives is the calendar-time half and the reporting practice.
problems.statement: Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person eligible at many points contributes to many of them. The resulting within-person dependence has been addressed: clustering by person, and confidence-interval procedures for survival outcomes compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, which covers better in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. What has not been addressed is the calendar-time structure. Trials begun at different times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so a pooled estimate assumes an effect common to start times that differ in all three. Trial start is not conventionally modeled flexibly, treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity is not conventionally examined, and trial-specific estimates are not reported alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible starts is invisible.
problems.why_open: Testing the common-effect assumption costs the efficiency the design was adopted for, since trial-specific estimates are individually imprecise by construction. A person's later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so the trials are linked causally rather than only statistically, and whether that is innocuous depends on the outcome model being correct, which is the thing under test. Reporting per-start estimates also complicates a paper whose selling point was a single efficient number.
problems.proposed_direction: Model trial start flexibly rather than adjusting it away, examine treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity, and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible start times is visible. Cluster by person as standard, and use a person-level bootstrap where uncertainty from the estimated weights is material rather than assuming the sandwich estimator suffices. Establish whether the efficiency gain survives the correct variance treatment, since the case for the design has usually been made under the naive variance.

prior_work.cite: Causal inference in survival analysis using longitudinal observational data: sequential trials and marginal structural models. Stat Med 2023
prior_work.what_it_does: Sets out the sequential-trials estimator alongside marginal structural models for survival outcomes.
